headline: Peanut Bunker Piling Into the Coves — Bass Waiting Until Dark to Eat Them
subhead: The bait's thick from Oyster Bay to Charles Island, but the bite window has shrunk to first light and last light as the Sound settles into a warm, slack neap.
body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning just watching before I even rigged a rod. That's the job half the time — find the bait, let it tell you where to be. And this week the bait is everywhere. Peanut bunker have packed into the coves from Oyster Bay to Northport, balled up tight against the shoreline in three and four feet of water, nervous, flickering on the surface like they know something's under them. Off Charles Island the bay anchovies and silversides are so thick the water looks like it's got a texture to it — almost oily on a calm morning. That's the tell. When the bait gets that dense and that shallow, the predators aren't far, they're just not always showing themselves.

And that's been the story of the week — the bait's here, the fish are here, but they're not eating on your schedule. Kings Point is reading just under 71 degrees, New London's a couple degrees cooler at 69.4, and that gradient across the Central Sound basin means the western half — Oyster Bay through Norwalk — is running warmer than anything east of Stratford Shoal. Warm water plus a bright July sun plus a first-quarter neap tide sliding in this week has pushed the bass into a low-light and after-dark pattern almost everywhere I've fished. Daytime, you might mark them on the bunker schools but they sit under the bait sulking, not committing. Dawn and dusk, and especially the two hours after dark, they turn on.

The better bass reports this week have come off Eatons Neck and the mouth of Northport Bay, working peanut bunker schools with a bucktail-and-teaser combo — half-ounce white bucktail with a 4-inch white or bunker-colored soft plastic trailer, cast right into the edge of the bait ball and let it sink before the retrieve. Guys working live bunker on a fish-finder rig off Middle Ground Light have had better luck right at last light into the first hour of dark, drifting the edge where the shoal drops from 20 feet down into the channel. The neap tide is softening the current through there — less water moving means the rip off Stratford Shoal isn't ripping the way it does on a full or new moon, so the drift is slower and the strike zone stays open longer. That's actually working in our favor for eel and swimbait guys — wider bite windows even if the total number of fish holding on the structure is down a touch from peak spring current.

Fluke have been the most dependable thing going in Central Sound the last ten days, and that hasn't changed. The Norwalk Islands drift — anywhere from Sheffield to the Chimon Island flats — has been holding fluke to 5 pounds on the incoming tide, best on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged behind a 3/4-ounce bucktail, dragged slow over the sand-to-mussel-bed transitions in 15 to 25 feet. Off Port Jefferson, the channel edges out toward the Middle Ground have been giving up keeper fluke too, mixed with a lot of shorts, which tells me there's a strong young class coming through behind this year's keepers. Squid strips on the bucktail have been outproducing plain Gulp when the current is really moving, which makes sense — more scent in faster water.

Porgies are holding up well on the rock piles and mussel beds around Charles Island and the western edge of Stratford Shoal — small hooks, sandworms or clam, fished right on bottom in 20 to 35 feet, and you don't need to move much once you find them stacked. Blackfish season's still weeks off in most of the state waters here, so I haven't chased them, but the structure they'll eventually load onto is already thick with crabs, which is a good early sign for the fall opener. Weakfish have been a ghost this year in the numbers I'd expect — a few incidental fish mixed into the fluke drifts around the Norwalk Islands, nothing you could call a pattern yet.

We flagged bonito working into Western Sound ten days back, and I've had my eye on the bait for exactly that reason — tight, fast-moving anchovy and silverside schools are the setup those fish love. Nothing confirmed yet on this side of the Norwalk Islands, but the ingredients are lining up: warm water, dense small bait, and a west-to-east gradient that funnels things our direction as August nears. I wouldn't be surprised to hear the first Central Sound bonito report within the next week or two.

Looking ahead, the neap tide keeps easing through the weekend, which should keep the Stratford Shoal and Middle Ground drifts more forgiving for eel and bucktail guys working after dark. If I had one trip this week, I'd fish the last light bite off Eatons Neck into full dark on bunker-imitating soft plastics, then swing over to the Norwalk Islands the next morning on the incoming for fluke. Watch the bait before you pick a spot — right now it's doing more talking than the fish are.
